body:
## Problem

`isPanicking()` in `internal/internal_workflow.go:1043` calls `runtime.Callers()` + `runtime.CallersFrames()` on every invocation to check if `runtime.gopanic` is on the call stack. This function is called from `coroutineState.yield`, which executes on every workflow coroutine yield point.

Under load (throughput_stress benchmark, mc1000, 1 min), this single function accounts for:
- **14.3% of total CPU time** (4.49s of 31.34s in a 30s CPU profile)
- **10.2% of total allocations** (254 MB of 2.43 GB)

The allocations come from:
- `[20]uintptr` array for `runtime.Callers()` — 81 MB
- `runtime.CallersFrames()` iterator — 125 MB  
- `frames.Next()` frame copies — 48 MB

The stack unwinding (`runtime.step`, `pcvalue`, `Frames.Next`) also dominates the CPU profile at ~22%.

## Profiling data

```
ROUTINE ======================== go.temporal.io/sdk/internal.isPanicking
  254.04MB   254.04MB (flat, cum) 10.19% of Total
         .          .   1043:func isPanicking() bool {
   81.01MB    81.01MB   1044:	var pcs [20]uintptr
         .          .   1045:	n := runtime.Callers(1, pcs[:])
  125.03MB   125.03MB   1046:	frames := runtime.CallersFrames(pcs[:n])
         .          .   1047:	for {
      48MB       48MB   1048:		frame, more := frames.Next()
         .          .   1049:		if frame.Function == "runtime.gopanic" {
```

CPU callers:
```
     0.04s  0.13%      4.49s 14.33%  | go.temporal.io/sdk/internal.isPanicking
                       2.91s 64.81%  |   runtime.(*Frames).Next
                       1.41s 31.40%  |   runtime.Callers (inline)
```

## Suggestion

Consider one of:
1. Use `recover()` to detect panics instead of stack walking
2. Set a goroutine-local flag when entering panic handling rather than probing the stack every yield
3. Allow disabling via `WorkerOptions` (e.g., `DeadlockDetectionTimeout` set to a very large value already exists but doesn't skip `isPanicking`)

## Environment

- SDK version: v1.42.0
- Go: go1.26.2
- Scenario: omes `throughput_stress` with mc1000
- OS: Linux amd64
title: isPanicking() uses 14% CPU and 10% allocations due to runtime.Callers() on every coroutine yield
